title: "Benchmark: H3 package and the cost of geocoding"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = TRUE)
results <- function(name) {
  path <- file.path("..", "..", "bench", "results", paste0(name, ".parquet"))
  tibble::as_tibble(arrow::read_parquet(path))
}
backends <- results("h3-backends")
inside <- results("h3-inside-rows")
bench_script <- file.path("..", "..", "bench", "h3-backends.R")
(knitr::read_chunk)(bench_script)
```

This article reads stored results; it does not run the benchmark. The script
is `bench/h3-backends.R`; its code is shown below as it was run.

## Question

The geospatial encoding needs, for every row, the H3 cells of the four
corners of its bounding box, and for the rows that cross cell edges the
cells whose centre lies inside the polygon and the cell polygons. Two R
packages offer these operations: `h3o` (Rust) and `h3jsr` (JavaScript through
V8). Which is faster on the package's own workload, do they agree, and what
does geocoding cost per row once one is chosen?

A second question comes from the plan's open points: a row whose four box
corners fall in one cell is treated as lying inside that cell. Box edges
along parallels are not great circles, so how often does such a row reach
into another cell, by row size and latitude?

## Results

```{r}
shown <- backends[c("case", "expression", "points", "median_s", "min_s", "max_s", "us_per_item")]
shown$median_s <- signif(shown$median_s, 3)
shown$min_s <- signif(shown$min_s, 3)
shown$max_s <- signif(shown$max_s, 3)
shown$us_per_item <- signif(shown$us_per_item, 3)
knitr::kable(shown)
```

`points` counts the items of each operation: box corners, crossing polygons,
distinct cells, or rows for `encode_h3o`. Both packages return the same cell
for every corner: `corners_agree` is `r all(backends$corners_agree)` in every
case.

```{r}
ratio <- function(case, op) {
  rows <- backends[backends$case == case, ]
  rows$median_s[rows$expression == paste0(op, "_h3jsr")] /
    rows$median_s[rows$expression == paste0(op, "_h3o")]
}
speedup <- expand.grid(case = unique(backends$case), operation = c("corners", "polyfill", "boundaries"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
speedup$h3jsr_over_h3o <- round(mapply(ratio, speedup$case, speedup$operation), 1)
knitr::kable(speedup)
```

## Verdict

```{r, include = FALSE}
largest <- backends[backends$rows == max(backends$rows), ]
per_row_us <- 1e6 * largest$median_s[largest$expression == "encode_h3o"] / max(backends$rows)
```

- `h3o` is the H3 package of `rcs`. It is faster than `h3jsr` on every
  operation measured, by the factors in the table above, and gives the same
  cells. `h3jsr` is not needed.
- Geocoding costs about `r round(per_row_us, 1)` microseconds per row on
  `r format(max(backends$rows), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` polygons
  (whole `geo_encode()`, one worker). The corner cells take
  `r round(100 * largest$median_s[largest$expression == "corners_h3o"] / largest$median_s[largest$expression == "encode_h3o"])`%
  of it; most of the rest goes to the crossing rows (about 15% of the
  simulated rows): candidate cells, the spherical intersection test and the
  intersection areas.
- Inside rows: `r sum(inside$violations)` of `r format(sum(inside$inside), big.mark = ",")`
  inside rows had a boundary point in another cell. The package nevertheless
  tests extra points along the edge nearest the equator when the bend of
  that parallel could exceed 1 cm (`geo_edge_points()`); a box that fails
  becomes a crossing row.

## Limits

- One machine, local disk, one worker; `rcs.workers > 1` is not measured
  here.
- `h3o`'s `"intersect"` mode, which would give the cells a polygon touches in
  one call, misses the cell of a polygon lying inside one cell, and returns
  too few cells for a polygon around a pole (71 of 338 at resolution 5 for
  the simulated pole row; for the antimeridian row 403 of 404, with or
  without splitting the shape at 180 degrees). The package therefore finds touched cells from
  boundary points, their first ring and the cells whose centre is inside,
  tests each candidate on the sphere with `s2`, and descends the H3
  hierarchy for shapes across the antimeridian or around a pole. These steps
  are part of `encode_h3o`, but not of the per-package comparison.
- The inside-row measure samples box edges at 64 points; a reach shorter
  than that spacing between two sample points would go unseen.
